title: Ranked staff shortlists in project software, with the resource manager deciding
problem: Resource managers match people to roles from memory, spreadsheets and phone calls, so familiarity shapes who is picked and people with the right skills elsewhere are overlooked.
approach: An agent in the firm's project system proposes ranked candidates from skills, availability and cost data; a resource manager confirms or overrides.
Named uses include Basware (on Kantata), Nextview and Diabsolut (Certinia agents), and zeb, whose agent proposes and pre-books people.
Kantata states customers see a 40% improvement in resource planning accuracy (vendor-published); no acceptance or override rate for shortlists was found.
who: Basware, Nextview, Diabsolut, zeb; Kantata, Certinia

title: McKinsey plans AI agents to help match consultants to client teams
problem: McKinsey's professional-development staff have matched consultants to clients for decades, and the process has become more complex as the firm grew to almost 40,000 employees.
approach: Bloomberg Law reports McKinsey plans to use AI agents to help choose the consultants assigned to client teams.
Agents supplement rather than replace the professional-development staff.
No result, pilot size or timeline is published (self-reported).

title: Client emails and statements of work turned into roles and suggested assignments
problem: Someone reads client requests by email and portal, copies them into the pipeline and checks with managers, and may not reply the same day; kickoff preparation takes days.
approach: Cinode's MailMatch reads emails, portal links and attachments to extract roles, skills and dates, creates a pipeline project and runs semantic matching.
Rocketlane's Workforce Agent turns a statement of work into a draft plan with suggested assignments; no automatic booking is described.
Rocketlane says kickoff preparation compresses from days to hours (vendor-published); no baseline given. A staffer reviews Cinode matches and books.

title: Rolling demand and capacity forecast by role and skill, with what-if scenarios
problem: Pipeline and capacity sit in separate tools, so forecasts are quarterly at best, and 55% of firms in a Dayshape survey miss, delay or turn down work over capacity.
approach: Pipeline and capacity feed a rolling forecast using win rates and seasonality, showing where demand exceeds supply by role, skill and period.
Kantata customer Hakkoda moved from forecasting four weeks ahead to three to six months ahead (vendor-published).
Vendor claims: Kantata lists a 10% absolute improvement in average project margin; Deltek states a 20% improvement in forecast accuracy (vendor-published).
The operations leader reviews the forecast and decides hiring, contracting and bids; no source describes automatic triggers.

title: Staffing scenarios compared across projects, with margin impact shown at decision time
problem: Staffing choices are made with the financial consequence invisible until a later review.
approach: Kantata's Staffing Optimizer models scenarios across projects; Candidate Assignments compares internal and external resources on skills, availability and margin impact.
Projectworks describes margin impact appearing when a contractor is added or the seniority mix changed.
No results published; the operations leader or resource manager chooses among scenarios.

title: Agent re-matches people and proposes replacements for work in flight
problem: Replacing a person mid-project means finding every assignment and searching for a match on the same criteria and timeframes, and managers scramble without pipeline visibility.
approach: Certinia's Reallocation Agent finds a person's assignments and proposes best-match replacements on the same criteria and timeframes to resource managers.
Rocketlane's Resource Management Agent, in active rollout, flags people nearing over-capacity and ranks reallocation options by delivery impact and margin fit.
The agent proposes options and a resource manager decides; no measured outcome or override rate is published.

title: Bench gaps detected early and matched to open or unsold work
problem: Consultants sit idle between projects while the person staffing work does not see them, and the same people get tapped repeatedly.
approach: Rocketlane describes an agent that flags a bench gap when allocation falls below target for the next two to three weeks.
Kantata's Skills Profiling on Unsold Work lets firms soft-book people before contracts are signed and see skills gaps early.
Certinia claims reduced bench time but publishes no figure (vendor-published); the agent surfaces gaps and a manager redeploys.

title: Continuous utilisation and overallocation monitoring with early alerts
problem: Utilisation problems are found in last month's report, after starting weeks earlier; average billable utilisation fell to 66.4% in 2025, the lowest in SPI Research's survey history.
approach: A background process flags risks early, such as hours above target for two consecutive weeks or a team below a utilisation threshold.
Rocketlane describes checks flagging anyone booked over 100% across several weeks; Deltek says its Dela uses machine learning on past project performance.
Baseline, not a result: utilisation fell from 68.9% in 2024 to 66.4% in 2025; top-maturity firms exceed 80% (vendor-published).
The operations leader acts on alerts; alert-to-action practice is not described.

title: Conversational resourcing assistant answers who has the skills and capacity
problem: Answering who has this experience and capacity in July takes a morning of phone calls and spreadsheet checks, and staffing often depends on one or two people.
approach: Natural-language questions run over project data; assistants can also flag resource conflicts or draft a plan from a statement of work.
Kantata launched Expertise Agent on 2026-06-16; Rocketlane markets a Nitro Resource Management Agent; Certinia lists an Ask Veda Agent.
Projectworks says a question that took a morning returns in seconds (illustrative; vendor-published). The person asking decides.

title: Skills inventory kept current from profiles, project history and role descriptions
problem: Self-reported skills profiles say little about how recently a skill was used or proficiency, and 45% of law firms in BigHand's survey had only partial skills data.
approach: Cinode's AI suggests skills for a role from its title and description and matches related skills rather than exact keywords.
Deltek describes certification tracking with skill-based matching; TSIA's first maturity level has AI update profiles from project data.
No outcome published for skills upkeep; 67.7% of respondents chose skills intelligence as their second most-wanted AI support (vendor-published).

title: One matching view across employees, subcontractors, candidates and partner consultants
problem: Many systems match only internal employees, while firms use subcontractors and partners to fill gaps; subcontractors contributed 10.4% of revenue in SPI's 2025 benchmark.
approach: Cinode matches employees, subcontractors, candidates and partner consultants in one view and can post unfilled roles to partners.
Kantata compares internal and external resources side by side on skills, availability and margin impact.
A staffer chooses and books; no results published.

title: Central skills-based resourcing with open opportunity boards in place of partner-led allocation
problem: Work was allocated by partners calling around, so lawyers could lack capacity when deadlines moved, and BigHand's survey found 37% of firms say partners resource on personal preference.
approach: Womble Bond Dickinson and DLA Piper use central resourcing teams and opportunities boards where associates volunteer for open requests.
Reed Smith's tool is decision support, so staffing decisions stay with people; Deutsche Telekom planned Eightfold matching, piloting with about 1,000 people.
DLA Piper reports time saved finding resources: 600+ hours (about GBP 673,000 in stated value) (vendor-published).
who: Womble Bond Dickinson, DLA Piper, Reed Smith

title: Algorithm assigns cases to analysts instead of managers (randomised public-agency trial)
problem: Assigning legally complex, deadline-bound cases to analysts is a matching problem between case complexity and skill, and managers use soft information about who fits which case.
approach: Peru's environmental enforcement agency (OEFA) tested replacing manager assignment with case lists from a linear-optimisation algorithm, not machine learning.
Analysts given algorithm-selected cases were about 5 percentage points less likely to conclude a case on time (control about 40%) (independent).
No human checkpoint in the automated arm, by design; fines, appeal rates and appeal outcomes did not differ (independent).

title: Suggested completion dates shown on cases while managers keep assignment (randomised trial)
problem: Analysts working a backlog of deadline-bound cases need cues on sequencing, and managers kept the assignment decision but lacked a scheduling prompt.
approach: The same OEFA system displayed suggested completion dates on randomly chosen cases, leaving case selection with managers or the algorithm.
Suggested completion dates raised timely completion by about 4 percentage points, mostly among manager-assigned cases (independent).
Managers keep case selection in the manager-assigned arm; dates are suggestions.

title: One professional with AI instead of a two-person team (field experiment)
problem: Team composition rules assume AI is absent; if AI replaces some benefits of collaboration, staffing two people on a task may add cost without adding quality.
approach: Staff a single professional with AI where a pair would have been used.
A pre-registered Procter & Gamble experiment randomly assigned 776 professionals to work with or without AI, alone or in two-person teams.
Individuals with AI matched the performance of teams without AI (independent).
The experiment compares conditions; it is not a documented staffing policy.

title: AI agents planned, allocated and costed alongside people as assignable capacity
problem: Capacity planning assumed people and hourly rates, yet 87% of 200 leaders plan to use AI agents in their workforce.
approach: Planview announced Agent Resource Management to plan, govern and cost human and agent capacity, with availability from Fall 2026.
TSIA's third maturity level optimises work across consultants, subcontractors, partners and AI agents in one model.
No surveyed organisation has agents operational as assignable resources; 10.7% run formal pilots (vendor-published).
Accountability stays with humans, per Certinia; how a resource manager signs off agent assignments is not described.

title: Experienced flexible talent covers overflow and helps train and review AI tools
problem: Associates under billable pressure choose client work over AI training even when offered credit, and knowledge teams lack subject-matter experts to train tools and review output.
approach: Firms bring in experienced attorneys to cover overflow and to help train internal AI tools and review AI-generated work.
A sponsored accounting article recommends contract talent as a planned part of busy-season capacity.
The provider says one law firm has dozens of its attorneys working for one rainmaker; no firm named, no metrics (vendor-published).
Flexible lawyers review AI-generated work and do quality control.

title: In-house legal teams move work in-house as AI lifts internal capacity
problem: In-house legal teams decide what to do internally and what to send to outside counsel, and AI changes what internal teams can absorb.
approach: Corporate legal departments insource work that generative AI makes manageable internally, reducing reliance on outside counsel for it.
The survey records expectations, not a measured shift: 64% of in-house respondents expect to rely less on outside counsel (vendor-published).
78% of respondents see an opportunity to insource drafting (contract management 71%, research 62%) (vendor-published).
The decision to insource or outsource a matter stays with the legal department.

title: Idea: feed delivery outcomes back into staffing decisions
problem: Idea, not a deployment: resource managers support outcome-oriented delivery without outcome data, as only 7.3% of Resource Management Institute respondents say it is easily accessible and routinely used.
approach: Idea: feed delivery outcomes (margin, client result, risk) back into staffing so recommendations reflect which people and agent combinations produce strong results.
73.4% of respondents say this knowledge would be very or extremely valuable (vendor-published).
Kantata's October 2025 release described a planned Sales Accelerator using delivery history to propose optimal human-AI resource mixes.
Deal staffing stays with resource managers in the source's framing.

title: Idea: check whether AI freed capacity, then reset capacity plans
problem: Idea, not a deployment: capacity models convert demand into hours, but a columnist argues AI intensifies work so freed capacity gets refilled.
approach: Idea: audit whether hours actually fell after AI adoption, check effort assumptions against measured hours and demand, and reset plans.
Demand for Big Law hours rose 4.2% in the first half of 2026 against about 1.5% normal growth (independent).
SPI Research calls the gap between time AI saves and revenue it generates the leak; no source names a tool for this.

title: Idea: decision log, disparate-impact testing and explanations for AI-assisted staffing
problem: Idea, not a deployment: rules naming work allocation are arriving, yet only 4% of Resource Management Institute respondents name ethical or compliance concerns as a gap.
approach: Idea: record each AI staffing recommendation and the human decision, test for disparate impact, and explain the AI's role to affected people.
Controls come from legal texts and codes; no firm was found operating this, and no source reports override or acceptance rates.
Cited checkpoints: a reviewer who can change the decision, and a qualified individual able to override or discontinue a high-risk AI system.
